nameStory: This lichen's scientific name 'afrorevoluta' hints at its distinctive rolled-back edges, with 'revoluta' meaning 'rolled backward' in Latin. The 'afro' part of its name refers to its discovery and initial description from African specimens, though it's found in other regions too. Like other loop lichens in its genus, it gets its common group name from the characteristic way its lobes curve and overlap, creating loop-like patterns.
description: **[Note: This is a very rare species with limited observations - identification should be verified by experts]** This is a medium-sized foliose (leaf-like) lichen that forms grayish-green rosettes on tree bark. It belongs to the loop lichen group, characterized by broad, flat lobes that curl backward at the edges, creating a distinctive rolled appearance. Individual colonies can spread 2-4 inches across, with the lobes overlapping in an almost flower-like pattern. The upper surface has a somewhat papery texture when dry.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms circular rosettes of broad, flat lobes that curve backward at the edges, creating a distinctive rolled or revolute margin that you can see clearly from the side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to bluish-gray on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; underside is typically black with pale edges

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth and somewhat papery when dry, becoming softer and more pliable when moistened

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on bark of deciduous trees, particularly favoring smooth-barked species like maples and birches

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies typically 2-4 inches across, with lobes about 0.2-0.4 inches wide

habitat: Found on the bark of deciduous trees in mixed and deciduous forests throughout New England, though extremely uncommon with only a handful of confirmed observations. Prefers trees with relatively smooth bark in areas with good air quality, often in mature forest settings. Most likely to be encountered in protected woodlands away from urban pollution.

seasonality.spring: Visible on tree bark as grayish rosettes; frequent spring rains will show the dramatic color change to bright green when wet.
seasonality.summer: During dry spells appears more grayish and papery; thunderstorms reveal the vibrant green wet coloration most dramatically.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible as leaves drop, making tree bark inspection easier; wet fall weather brings out green colors against colorful autumn foliage.
seasonality.winter: Most easily spotted against snow-covered bark; appears grayish-brown when dry but still shows characteristic rolled lobe edges.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it's been confirmed in only three locations across the entire region - making it rarer here than some orchids or endangered birds, yet it quietly grows unnoticed on tree bark where most people would never think to look!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other loop lichens, especially Powdered Loop Lichen, but the strongly rolled-back lobe edges are more pronounced in this species. The rolled margins create distinct shadows that make the edges appear almost tubular rather than flat - imagine tiny gray-green scrolls attached to the bark.
contextualKnowledge: With only three recorded observations in all of New England, this species represents one of our region's rarest lichens. Any suspected sighting should be photographed and reported to local naturalist groups, as new discoveries could significantly expand our understanding of its distribution.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives, this species has more dramatically rolled lobe margins than Powdered Loop Lichen and lacks the powdery soredia (reproductive dust) found on Powder-tipped Antler Lichen. The rolled edges are the key distinguishing feature - they're so pronounced they create distinct shadows along the lobe margins, unlike the flatter edges of most other loop lichens.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its loop lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Antler Lichen has the narrowest, most antler-like lobes and the most abundant powdery soredia.
Unlike its relative the Powder-tipped Antler Lichen which has more irregular, branching lobes, Clingy Square Britches maintains those characteristic square-shaped segments.
Powdered Loop Lichen differs from Powder-tipped Antler Lichen by having broader, more rounded lobes rather than narrow, branching ones.
Unlike Powder-tipped Antler Lichen which has white powdery patches along its edges, Showman's Loop Lichen maintains a clean, smooth surface.
